idea: A bar chart of English letter frequencies, bars sorted tallest to shortest, with only the twelve letters along the axis reading ETAOIN SHRDLU. Linotype keyboards were laid out roughly by frequency, and operators ran a finger down the first two columns to fill a botched line, so 'etaoin shrdlu' sometimes got printed in newspapers by mistake. Type nerds will spot the in-joke.

A log-log scatter plot of every word in Moby-Dick ranked by how often it appears, with the dots falling into an almost straight diagonal line, captioned 'Zipf's law. Nobody agreed to it.' It shows a strange pattern that turns up in every language studied, drawn as one clean line.

42 rows of tiny plotted dashes set in two columns like a page with the words removed, captioned '42 lines. Mainz, c. 1455.' It's a minimalist tribute to the Gutenberg Bible, which is known as the 42-line Bible for how many lines it has in each column.

All the punctuation in Pride and Prejudice, with every word taken out, set in order as one long spiral of commas, semicolons and dashes, captioned 'Pride and Prejudice, words removed.' Readers can wear an author's rhythm as a fingerprint.

One continuous line drawn by a program across a QWERTY keyboard layout, visiting each key in the order needed to type 'The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog', with that sentence set small underneath. It's a sentence built only to contain all 26 letters, turned into a tangled, pretty path.

One sentence made up by a simple Markov chain trained on a dictionary's definitions, set in a sober serif and captioned 'Statistically plausible. Meaning not included.' It's a sharp, timely comment on text generated by machines.

A lowercase 'a' drawn as raw pen-stroke paths with every control point and coordinate label showing, captioned 'A letter is a program. (Knuth, METAFONT)'. It celebrates Donald Knuth's system that describes typefaces as code instead of drawings.

A large ampersand built from Bézier curves with its handles and anchor points drawn in, captioned 'and per se and'. Schoolchildren once recited '&' at the end of the alphabet with that phrase, and over time it slurred into the word 'ampersand'.

A neat 8x8 grid showing all 64 possible six-dot Braille cells (the blank one included), generated in order, captioned 'Six dots. Sixty-four possibilities. Louis Braille was fifteen.' He published his system in 1824, at about that age, and the grid makes the combinatorics plain.

The alphabet in Morse code drawn as horizontal bars and sorted by length, with E alone as a single dot at the top, captioned 'E is shortest because a printer had the most E's.' Alfred Vail is said to have set the code lengths by counting the type in a newspaper's type cases.

A blank two-page book spread with the Van de Graaf canon's construction lines drawn in, the diagonals that fix the text block and margins, captioned 'The margins were solved before the software.' Book designers and anyone who loves a well-made page will get it.

A radial tree of the Indo-European languages drawn from data, with the word for 'mother' at each tip and a caption collecting a few: 'mother · Mutter · mater · mḗtēr · mātṛ'. It shows thousands of years of shared ancestry in a single word.

A dense network graph in which every node is a dictionary headword and every edge points to a word used in its definition, with one closed loop picked out in bold, captioned 'Every word is defined by other words.' It's a quietly philosophical piece for people who think about meaning.

The standard 'Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet' paragraph with plotted arrows linking it back to its source line in Cicero's De finibus ('...neque porro quisquam est qui dolorem ipsum...'), captioned 'Placeholder text, cut from Cicero, 45 BC.' Designers use it every day, and few know it comes from a real passage about pain.

One sentence repeated down the shirt with more of its letters removed by a program on each line, still readable well past the point you'd expect, captioned 'Shannon estimated English is about half redundant.' It's information theory you can test with your own eyes.

A map of Europe drawn only as dots, one for each town that had a printing press by 1500, sized by how many editions it printed, captioned 'Fifty years after Gutenberg.' It shows how quickly a single invention spread.

A vowel chart plotted from real formant measurements (F1 against F2), with the dots of spoken vowels clustering into the familiar tilted trapezoid, captioned 'Your mouth is a map.' It's a phonetics fact that also works as an abstract graphic.

One hundred lowercase 'g's from a hundred different typefaces, outlined and stacked on top of each other into a ghostly average, captioned 'Same letter. Different opinions.' It's a love letter to type design and how much variety one letter can hold.

A block of justified text with a program tracing the 'rivers' of white space that run down through the gaps between words as flowing lines, captioned 'Rivers: what typesetters fight.' It turns a flaw that typographers hate into something lovely to look at.

A crisp Reed-Kellogg sentence diagram of 'Call me Ishmael.' with its baseline, the understood subject '(you)' and the slanted line for the object complement, and the sentence underneath. It's a grammar-class flashback for anyone who loves Melville.
